summary: JavaVulBench is a Java method-level vulnerability-detection dataset (30,637 methods: 5,281 vulnerable, 4,964 patched, 20,392 negatives; 1,740 CVEs, 700+ projects, 225 CWEs, 2015-2025) with line labels and five shipped split strategies, plus a harness that runs encoder classifiers, Ollama-served and OpenRouter-served LLMs through one prediction schema. It ships a per-model contamination audit that splits test CVEs by model training cutoff.

claims.claim: Switching from random to project-disjoint split reproduces on Java the 15-40 F1-point gap reported for C/C++
claims.evidence: Table 1: UniXcoder 0.446 -> 0.298 (-14.8 pts), GraphCodeBERT 0.343 -> 0.256 (-8.7 pts); CodeBERT 0.422 -> 0.000 is a degenerate majority-class collapse at threshold 0.5; DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B 0.341 -> 0.062. Only two of four models show a non-degenerate drop and neither is within 15-40 points, so the 'reproduces' wording is overstated, though the direction holds.

claims.claim: Twelve detectors evaluated under identical conditions from one command
claims.evidence: Table 2 (4 models, full project split N=4,167) and Table 3 (8 API LLMs on a 200-sample stratified probe, seed 42). The two tables are explicitly not one leaderboard; API LLMs see only 200 samples, single seed, no CIs.

claims.claim: Contamination audit separates memorized from unseen CVEs; strongest API models score higher on the clean subset
claims.evidence: Table 4: e.g. GPT-4o F1 0.488 all vs 0.528 clean; Claude Sonnet 4 0.444 vs 0.480. Audit is a date-vs-cutoff heuristic, not evidence of memorization; differences are on 200-sample probes without variance.
§5: Zenodo archive with data (CC-BY-4.0), code (MIT), predictions, fine-tuned checkpoints, Docker, staged reproduce.py; cached pipeline 30-45 min.

patterns.note: New Java benchmark with leakage-aware reporting; argues split strategy must be reported with every number.
Evaluates learned/LLM vulnerability detectors as an analysis signal; F1 at most ~0.42-0.53 on probes, i.e. not reliable as a gate.

methodology.sample: 30,637 Java methods; project split test N=4,167; time split test N=12,139; API LLMs on a 200-sample probe
methodology.baselines: CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B fine-tuned; 8 zero-shot API/open-weight LLMs; no specialized SAST tools (CodeQL, Semgrep, SpotBugs) or prior detectors like IRIS
methodology.variance: Single run; single 200-sample seed for API models; no CIs
methodology.ablations: Split strategies act as the main controlled variable; no prompt ablations for LLMs
methodology.contamination_controls: Per-model risky/clean partition by CVE date vs model cutoff; deduplicated split currently equivalent to random at Jaccard 0.8 (admitted)

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; ACM template header names ASE 2026 but arXiv comment/journal_ref give no acceptance
standards.artifacts: Zenodo archive with data, code, checkpoints, prediction files, Docker; demo video

biases.detail: 'Reproduces the 15-40 F1-point gap' while measured non-degenerate drops are 8.7 and 14.8 points.
API LLMs evaluated on 200 samples only, single seed.
No repeated fine-tuning seeds or CIs; small F1 differences between API models are uninterpretable.
Date-vs-cutoff audit is a proxy; CVEs published after cutoff may have code present earlier in public repos; deduplicated split does not actually deduplicate.
No conventional static analyzers compared, so practitioners cannot tell whether LLM detectors add value over existing Java SAST.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Qwen, Meta models evaluated neutrally
coi.detail: Academic benchmark authors who do not ship a competing top-ranked detector.

verdict_reason: Strong artifact and a genuinely Java-specific dataset with useful split discipline, but the headline 'reproduces 15-40 points' is overstated, API LLM results rest on 200 samples with one seed, and it measures method-level classification rather than agentic coding. Admit as a Java security-evaluation resource, not as harness evidence.
applicability: One of few Java-specific resources in the corpus. For the team it is a ready dataset to measure whether an LLM security-review step in the harness catches OWASP-class flaws (deserialization, SSRF, path traversal, injection) that matter for content ingestion pipelines parsing external healthcare education packages. The numbers argue against using an LLM detector as a merge gate (F1 about 0.3-0.5 on project-disjoint data) and in favor of keeping deterministic SAST (Semgrep, local Sonar) as the gate, with LLM review advisory. Its split lesson transfers directly: evaluate any harness change on held-out repos (project-disjoint) rather than random task splits, which matters with >=4 ingestion repos. It says nothing about agent hosts, multi-repo coordination, or specs.
